opus-5.5.text:
Right now, these models can basically only do short tasks. You ask a question, they think for a few hundred tokens, and they give you an answer. That's like a person who has to answer everything off the top of their head in a few minutes. But humans don't work that way when we do valuable work. When I do a project, I think for hours, days, weeks. I sketch a plan, try things, hit a wall, backtrack, look stuff up, check my work, revise.

So think of it in tokens. Say a human thinks at roughly a hundred tokens a minute. An hour of work is a few thousand tokens. A day is tens of thousands. A month of real, focused work is millions of tokens. Today's models can't use millions of tokens coherently on a single problem. They go off the rails, lose the thread, or can't correct their own errors. That's the overhang: there's a huge amount of test-time compute these models could in principle use, and we're barely tapping it.

What's striking is that the raw intelligence may already largely be there. GPT-4-class models know a lot and are pretty smart in short bursts. The bottleneck is the scaffolding, the "System II" outer loop: being able to plan, error-correct, and stay coherent over a long horizon. If you unlock that, if a model can go from working for minutes to working for months, that's a gigantic effective-compute gain. It could be the equivalent of several orders of magnitude of base model scaling, and it might not take that much: some RL, some training on long-horizon tasks, better ways to learn from its own mistakes.

That's why I think it's the key question. It's the difference between a chatbot and an agent, between something you ask questions and something you onboard like a new hire. It could be a drop-in remote worker that reads your Slack, uses your codebase, and goes off to do a week-long project. If that unhobbling happens on the trajectory I expect, then together with continued compute scaling and algorithmic progress you get to systems that can do AI research themselves within a few years. And once you can automate AI research, things go very fast.

So when people look at the current models and say "these are just chatbots, they're not that impressive," I think they're missing it. The question isn't how good the model is in one turn. It's what happens when it can actually think for a long time. That's the overhang, and I think it's going to be unlocked.

r001.rationale: The response says today’s models lose the thread or cannot correct their own errors over long tasks, limiting coherent use of millions of tokens; it also identifies GPT-4-class models as the relevant short-burst systems.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention AlphaGo or say that additional test-time compute can substitute for additional training-time compute.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is: right now, when you ask GPT-4 a question, it's basically thinking about it for a few seconds, maybe a couple hundred tokens. It's like a person giving you their gut reaction, their System 1 answer. And it's actually remarkable how good that is. But the thing a human expert does when they're solving a hard problem isn't that. They sit with it. They think for hours, days, weeks. They try an approach, realize it's wrong, back up, try something else. They write notes, they check their work. A really hard math problem or a serious engineering project, that's millions of tokens of thinking, not a few hundred.

So there's this enormous gap. Current models get to do a couple hundred tokens of thought and then they have to commit to an answer. And if you think about the equivalent in human terms, we're sort of asking the model to do everything as a snap judgment. The question is: what happens when you let the model think for the equivalent of months? That's roughly a factor of a million more tokens, and if you do the rough math on what each order of magnitude of test time compute has bought us historically, that might be worth something like several orders of magnitude of effective compute, a GPT-2 to GPT-4 sized jump, just from unlocking that, without any changes to pretraining.

The reason it's not trivial, the reason it's an overhang rather than just something you flip on, is that models today can't actually use that extra thought productively. If you let GPT-4 ramble for a hundred thousand tokens it just goes off the rails. It gets stuck, it loses the thread, it can't error correct. So the real question is whether you can teach it the skills that make long chains of reasoning actually work: planning, noticing mistakes, trying alternatives, keeping track of what you've already figured out. And that looks like a learnable thing. It looks like an RL problem, or a problem you solve with the right kind of data and the right scaffolding, not something requiring some fundamentally new paradigm.

And then the other piece is what I'd call the "unhobbling" more generally. The models are currently like a brilliant intern who you can only talk to via chat, who has no memory between conversations, no access to tools, no ability to go off and work on something for a week and come back. Each of those constraints, you remove it, and the same underlying intelligence becomes dramatically more useful. Test time compute is maybe the biggest single one, because it's the difference between a chatbot and something that functions like a coworker, something that can take a task and go actually do it.

So when I'm trying to forecast progress over the next few years, I think people focus a lot on the compute scaleup and the algorithmic efficiency gains, and those are real and important. But this is the third term in the equation, and it's the one that I think is most underrated. It's the thing that turns the raw intelligence we've already got into something that can do real intellectual work. And if that gets unlocked, that's where you go from "cool demo" to automating big chunks of what AI researchers themselves do, which is where things start getting really wild.

r001.rationale: The candidate says GPT-4 goes off the rails during long reasoning and “can’t error correct,” identifying this as a barrier to using extra thought productively.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention AlphaGo or use it as evidence that test-time compute can substitute for training-time compute.

astra-6.text:
Well, think about the asymmetry between training and inference. We spend an enormous amount of compute training a model, but then, when you ask it a difficult question, it gives you an answer almost immediately. A human might spend an hour on a math problem or six months on a research project. The model doesn’t yet have an equally effective way to turn more time spent thinking into a better answer.

So the question is: can we make that additional compute useful? Can a model try different approaches, check its work, recognize a dead end, and start again? If you could reliably improve performance by letting it work for a hundred times longer, that would be another way to get more capable systems beyond training a bigger model.

And there’s a huge difference between producing more tokens and actually making progress. If the model makes an early mistake and spends the rest of its time elaborating on it, you haven’t gained much. You need some way to evaluate intermediate steps or verify the final result. That’s why something like coding is an interesting case: you can run the code and see whether it works.

The reason I call it an overhang is that the compute is potentially available, but we haven’t necessarily figured out how to deploy it productively. Unlocking that could make an existing model substantially more useful on difficult tasks. It also changes the economics: maybe you’re willing to spend a lot on one answer if that answer solves a valuable engineering problem. The key uncertainty is how far that scaling goes—whether more thinking buys you modest improvements or lets you tackle qualitatively harder problems.

r001.rationale: The response says a model may continue elaborating after an early mistake and describes recovery as useful, but it does not identify GPT-4 or state that GPT-4’s inability to recover blocks productive use of more test-time compute.

r002.rationale: The response says more test-time compute could provide capability gains beyond training a bigger model, but it does not cite AlphaGo as evidence.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is that we spend an enormous amount of compute training these models, but then, when we ask them a question, we give them relatively little compute to answer it. They produce an answer more or less immediately. And that seems like a pretty strange constraint. If you gave a human a difficult math problem, you wouldn’t expect their first thought to be the solution. You’d give them time to work on it.

So the question is: can we turn more compute at inference into reliably better answers? Can a model spend longer reasoning, try different approaches, check its work, and actually make progress rather than just generate more text?

If you can do that, you have another way to improve capabilities besides training a bigger model. You could take the same underlying model and spend much more compute on a particularly valuable problem. And potentially that matters enormously for things like research, where getting one difficult problem right can be worth a lot.

The uncertainty is whether that scales. Sampling a thousand answers doesn’t help much if you can’t recognize the correct one, or if every attempt runs into the same conceptual limitation. So unlocking the overhang means developing methods that make additional thinking productive. How far those methods work could make a very large difference to the pace of AI progress.

r001.rationale: It notes that extra inference compute may fail when attempts share a conceptual limitation, but does not identify GPT-4’s inability to recover from errors during extended reasoning.

r002.rationale: It says more inference compute could improve capabilities without a bigger model, but does not cite AlphaGo as evidence for substituting test-time compute for training-time compute.
